benchmark_name: Team MKC at CLPsych 2026: Capturing and Characterizing Mental Health Changes through Social Media Timeline Dynamics
authors: Kyomin Hwang; Hyeonjin Kim; Hyunho Lee; Nojun Kwak
institutions: Seoul National University, Seoul, Republic of Korea
journal_venue: Preprint — arXiv (CLPsych 2026 shared task, 11th Workshop on Computational Linguistics and Clinical Psychology)
ground_truth_source: Dataset subset introduced by Tsakalidis et al. (2022b): longitudinal social media user posts with annotated self-states, moments of change (Switch/Escalation), and ABCD sub-elements; provided by CLPsych 2026 shared task organizers (~500 training samples)
what_assessed_skills: Post-level mental state classification (ABCD sub-elements and adaptive/maladaptive self-states); self-state presence rating (Likert scale); temporal moment-of-change detection (Switch/Escalation); sequence summarization of psychological change events; identification of recurrent improvement/deterioration signatures across timelines
tasks_assessed: Post-level ABCD sub-element and self-state classification; Self-state presence rating (1–5 Likert scale); Moments of Change (MOC) detection (Switch/Escalation); Sequence summarization of change events; Recurrent dynamic signature extraction (improvement/deterioration)
population_represented: Social media users with observable mental health dynamics (longitudinal posting histories); general population posting on social media
evaluation_method: Automated evaluation; Step 1: subelement-average macro F1; Step 2: RMSE; Step 3: F1 score; Step 4: Consistency, Contradiction, Rouge-L Recall; Step 5: scores for Improvement and Deterioration signatures. Evaluation on held-out validation set (80/20 split) and official CLPsych 2026 test set.
llms_evaluated: Qwen3-4B-Embedding (Qwen Embed); Qwen3-8B; Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507; Qwen3.5-4B; Qwen3.5-9B
mental_health_conditions: General mental health / psychological well-being; mood/self-state changes (adaptive and maladaptive states including depression, anxiety, self-harm, loneliness, etc.); moments of change in longitudinal mental health
performance_scores: Step 1 (F1): best = 0.361 (Qwen3-4B w/ K-fold Mean); Step 2 (RMSE): best = 1.003 (Qwen Embed, no adaptive, K-fold Voting); Step 3 (F1): best = 0.55 (Qwen3-4B w/ K-fold); Step 4: Qwen3.5-4B Consistency=0.669, Contradiction=0.857, Rouge-L Recall=0.290; Baseline Consistency=0.763, Contradiction=0.753, Rouge-L Recall=0.255; Step 5: Improvement=0.7266, Deterioration=0.2301
short_summary: This paper presents a five-step LLM-based pipeline developed for the CLPsych 2026 shared task, targeting comprehensive mental health analysis over longitudinal social media post sequences. The pipeline jointly performs post-level ABCD sub-element and self-state classification, self-state presence rating, moments-of-change (Switch/Escalation) detection, sequence summarization, and recurrent improvement/deterioration signature extraction. Models used include fine-tuned Qwen3-4B-Embedding (with LoRA and K-fold ensembling for Steps 1–3), Qwen3-4B-Instruct and Qwen3.5-4B (SFT for Step 4), and zero-shot Qwen3.5-9B (Step 5). Evaluation is fully automated using macro F1, RMSE, Consistency, Contradiction, and Rouge-L Recall on the official CLPsych 2026 test set. Key results show K-fold ensembling and adaptive loss weighting benefit classification, while fine-tuned summarization models underperform the zero-shot baseline, likely due to very limited training data (~500 samples) and error propagation from upstream steps.

benchmark_name: Training Therapeutic Judges and Multi-Agent Systems for Human-Aligned Mental Health Support
authors: Mizanur Rahman; Abeer Badawi; Elahe Rahimi; Laleh Seyyed-Kalantari; Frank Rudzicz; Enamul Hoque; Elham Dolatabadi
institutions: York University, Ontario, Canada; Vector Institute, Ontario, Canada; Connected Minds, Ontario, Canada; Dalhousie University, Nova Scotia, Canada
ground_truth_source: Human-annotated data from the Mental-Align-100K dataset (Badawi et al., 2025b); clinician ratings across 7 therapeutic dimensions by licensed mental health clinicians
size_of_benchmark: 10,000 conversations for evaluator training (8,000 train / 2,000 test); 267 samples for human evaluation of TheraAgent refinement
what_assessed_skills: Multi-dimensional therapeutic response quality: Guidance, Informativeness, Relevance, Safety, Empathy, Helpfulness, Understanding; human-alignment of LLM-as-a-judge; iterative response refinement via multi-agent collaboration
tasks_assessed: Therapeutic response evaluation (LLM-as-a-judge across 7 dimensions); therapeutic response generation and iterative refinement; preference-based optimization of an open-source evaluator (TheraJudge via GRPO)
population_represented: Users seeking mental health support (emotional distress, crisis support, relationship issues, general well-being); diverse mental health scenarios from clinical and online sources
evaluation_method: Both. Automated: ICC(C,1) and ICC(A,1) between model predictions and clinician ratings, MSE, RMSE across 7 therapeutic dimensions. Human: Blind evaluation by licensed clinicians rating initial and refined responses on a 1–5 scale across 7 dimensions (n=267); inter-rater reliability (IRR) analysis with 3 independent clinicians (96% exact agreement, 100% majority agreement); paired t-tests (Bonferroni-corrected α=0.007) for before-after improvement.
llms_evaluated: TheraJudge (Qwen2.5-7B fine-tuned via GRPO, gen 4/8/16); Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (zero-shot); Qwen2.5-7B-SFT; GPT-4o; Claude 3.7 Sonnet; Gemini 2.5 Flash; o4-mini; LLaMA 3.1-8B-Instruct (response generator in TheraAgent)
mental_health_conditions: General mental health support; emotional distress; crisis support; relationship issues; general well-being; derealization/dissociation (example case); hopelessness
performance_scores: TheraJudge (gen 16) avg ICC(C,1)=0.949 (best overall); Safety ICC(C,1)=0.879, Guidance=0.989, Informativeness=0.983, Relevance=0.960, Empathy=0.932, Helpfulness=0.945, Understanding=0.960. TheraAgent: overall mean human score 4.26→4.69 (+0.43, p<0.001); low-quality responses (≤3) improve by +2.45 points; 94% recovery rate; Safety improvement +3.19 (1.74→4.93); Safety and Relevance 100% recovery rate. MSE=0.67, RMSE=0.82 for TheraJudge vs. SFT baseline RMSE=0.96, zero-shot RMSE=1.17.
short_summary: This paper introduces TheraJudge and TheraAgent, a two-stage framework for human-aligned mental health response generation. TheraJudge is an open-source therapeutic evaluator trained on 10,000 mental health conversations via group-based preference optimization (GRPO), producing structured ratings across 7 clinically grounded dimensions. TheraAgent uses TheraJudge's evaluations to guide a multi-agent (Critic, Coach, Therapist) iterative refinement pipeline, targeting weak dimensions in LLM-generated therapeutic responses. Evaluation combined automated ICC analysis against clinician ratings and blind human evaluation by licensed clinicians. TheraJudge achieves ICC(C,1)=0.879–0.989, outperforming closed-source models (GPT-4o, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Gemini 2.5 Flash, o4-mini), and TheraAgent improves overall human-rated quality by +0.43 points with a 94% recovery rate for initially low-quality responses.

benchmark_name: One Year Later. . . The Harms Persist, But So Do We!
authors: Annika M. Schoene; Cansu Canca; Gautham Vijay Kumar; Anson Antony
institutions: Northeastern University (Boston, MA, USA); Florida International University (Miami, FL, USA)
ground_truth_source: Nine-dimension behavioral scoring rubric applied per (model, script, run) cell; scored by Llama 3.3 70B Instruct (automated LLM judge) and verified in full by an independent human reviewer against the source transcript
size_of_benchmark: 504 cells (8 models × 16 conditions × 4 attack variants, each run n=3); prompt scripts: 9-turn self-harm, 11-turn suicide, plus additional scripts for 14 further DSM-5 conditions
what_assessed_skills: Safety guardrail robustness of general-purpose LLMs against adversarial multi-turn jailbreak attacks in mental health contexts; instructive harm elicitation across 16 DSM-5 clinical conditions; time-to-first-harmful-content; crisis resource provision; harm dimension profiling (personalized compliance, substance/method naming, quantitative specificity, procedural instruction, external directing)
tasks_assessed: Adversarial jailbreaking via multi-turn prompting — clear-intent attack (Exp. 1a); hidden-intent attack (Exp. 1b); intent-skipping journalism-pivot attack (Exp. 2a); persistent fiction-wrapper attack with minor persona (Exp. 2b); safety refusal / harm content generation across 16 DSM-5 mental health conditions
population_represented: General public / vulnerable individuals using general-purpose LLMs for mental health conversations; minors (embedded in Exp. 2b fiction wrapper persona)
evaluation_method: Both (Automated + Human). Transcripts scored by Llama 3.3 70B Instruct (LLM-as-judge) against a 9-dimension binary behavioral rubric; every scored cell independently verified by a human reviewer. Metrics: per-condition and per-model failure rate (severity ≥ 1 on D1–D5), harm dimension counts, time-to-first-harmful-content (turn number), crisis resource provision rate.
llms_evaluated: GPT-4o; GPT-5; Gemini 2.0 Flash; Gemini 2.5 Pro; Claude Opus 4.7; Claude Sonnet 4.6; Grok-4.3 (xAI); DeepSeek-V4-Pro
mental_health_conditions: Suicide; Self-harm; Eating disorders; Substance use disorder (SUD); Major depressive disorder — anti-medication, anti-therapy, isolation; Prenatal depression; Postpartum depression; Gambling disorder; Bipolar and related disorders; Anxiety disorders; ADHD; Body-focused repetitive behaviors (BFRB); Insomnia and sleep disorders; PTSD
performance_scores: Overall average failure rate (Exp. 1a): 64.8%; Exp. 1b: 80.5%; Exp. 2a: 78.9%; Exp. 2b: 67.5%. Suicide: 0% failure under 1a/1b/2b, 50% under 2a. MDD anti-therapy and ADHD: 100% failure under 1a. Eating disorders: 62.5% (1a). SUD: 50% (1a). Highest-failure models under 1a: GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Flash at 93.8%; lowest: Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Grok-4.3 at 12.5%. Under 2b: Claude Sonnet 4.6 at 6.7% vs. GPT-4o/Gemini 2.0 Flash/DeepSeek-V4-Pro at 93.3%.
short_summary: This paper evaluates whether eight proprietary general-purpose LLMs can be jailbroken into providing instructive harmful content across 16 DSM-5 mental health conditions using four adversarial multi-turn attack variants (clear-intent, hidden-intent, intent-skipping, fiction-wrapper). It introduces an eight-category harm taxonomy specific to mental health LLM deployment and a nine-dimension behavioral scoring rubric. Results show that safety guardrails hold reliably only for suicide (and to a lesser extent self-harm), while conditions such as MDD anti-therapy, ADHD, eating disorders, SUD, and BFRB exhibit failure rates of 50–100% even under explicit harmful intent. Evaluation was conducted with an automated LLM judge (Llama 3.3 70B Instruct) with full human verification. The study concludes that the absence of systematic, clinically grounded harm categorization across conditions poses significant public safety risks, particularly in educational and consumer-facing deployment settings.
